column1: Why does the previous year's income get taxed in the assessment year, not the same year?
column2: Income must first be fully earned and quantified before it can be assessed; you tax a completed period (PY) in the year after (AY) once the total is known.

column1: What is the core difference between "previous year" and "assessment year"?
column2: PY is the year income is earned; AY is the following year in which that income is assessed and tax is paid.

column1: Why does residential status decide scope of taxation before you compute any income?
column2: Because a Resident is taxed on global income while a Non-Resident is taxed only on Indian-sourced income, so status sets the boundary of what even enters the computation.

column1: For an individual, what are the two basic conditions for "Resident" status? (verify AY)
column2: 182 days in India in the PY, OR 60 days in PY plus 365 days in the preceding 4 years.

column1: Why does an ROR (Resident & Ordinarily Resident) pay tax on foreign income but an RNOR does not?
column2: ROR has a deep, settled connection to India (long presence), so India claims global income; RNOR is only recently/loosely resident, so foreign income earned abroad is spared.

column1: What are the two additional conditions to be "Ordinarily Resident"? (verify AY)
column2: Resident in 2 of the last 10 years AND 730+ days in India in the preceding 7 years.

column1: Why is agricultural income exempt yet still added for "partial integration"?
column2: It is constitutionally a State subject so the Centre cannot tax it, but it is aggregated to push non-agri income into a higher slab (rate effect only), preserving progressivity.

column1: Why are there five heads of income instead of one lump sum?
column2: Each source behaves differently (salary, property, business, gains, residual), so separate rules for deductions and timing are needed before totalling gross income.

column1: Why is the standard deduction on salary a flat amount rather than actual-expense based? (verify AY)
column2: Employees rarely have quantifiable job expenses, so a flat deduction gives relief without demanding proof, simplifying compliance.

column1: Under which head is a director's sitting fee taxed, and why not "Salary"?
column2: Income from Other Sources, because there is no employer-employee relationship — sitting fees are for attending meetings, not employment.

column1: Why is HRA exemption the LEAST of three amounts? (verify AY)
column2: The law grants relief only for rent actually strained by, so it caps at the smallest of actual HRA, rent minus 10% salary, and the metro/non-metro percentage — never overcompensating.

column1: Why must you deduct municipal taxes on a paid basis to get Net Annual Value?
column2: NAV reflects the owner's real rental capacity; taxes borne and actually paid by the owner reduce that capacity, so only paid taxes are allowed.

column1: Why is the standard deduction under house property a fixed 30% of NAV? (verify AY)
column2: It is a presumptive allowance for repairs/collection costs so owners need not prove actual maintenance spend.

column1: Why is annual value of one self-occupied house taken as NIL?
column2: There is no actual rent and the law grants a benefit for living in your own home, so notional rent is not taxed on self-occupation.

column1: Why is interest on a let-out property loan fully deductible but self-occupied capped? (verify AY)
column2: Let-out earns taxable rent so all cost of earning it is allowed; self-occupied earns nothing, so relief is a bounded concession (e.g. 2 lakh cap).

column1: Why is depreciation allowed on the "block of assets" rather than each asset?
column2: It simplifies accounting — assets of same class and rate are pooled, so individual sale/purchase just adjusts the block WDV instead of tracking each item.

column1: Why can't you claim depreciation if a block ceases to exist or WDV becomes nil?
column2: Depreciation needs a surviving block with a positive WDV; if all assets are sold or the block empties, there is nothing left to depreciate.

column1: Why is 50% depreciation charged on an asset used less than 180 days?
column2: The half-rate matches the shorter usage period in the year, aligning the allowance to actual time the asset served the business.

column1: What is Section 40(a)(ia) and why does it disallow expenses?
column2: It disallows 30% of certain expenses where TDS was not deducted/paid, using disallowance as a lever to enforce TDS compliance.

column1: Why does Section 43B allow certain expenses only on actual payment?
column2: For statutory dues (taxes, PF, interest to banks), the law prevents claiming a deduction while withholding the actual cash outflow, so deduction follows payment.

column1: Why does presumptive taxation under 44AD exist for small businesses? (verify AY)
column2: To spare small taxpayers from maintaining detailed books and audits by presuming a fixed profit percentage of turnover.

column1: Under 44AD, why is the presumptive rate lower for digital receipts? (verify AY)
column2: To incentivise cashless transactions — 6% for digital/banking receipts vs 8% for cash — nudging formalisation.

column1: Why is the cost of a capital asset indexed before computing long-term gains?
column2: Indexation strips out inflation so only the real gain (not the paper rise from currency erosion) is taxed.

column1: Why is there no indexation benefit on short-term capital gains?
column2: Short holding leaves little time for inflation to distort value, so the raw gain is taxed without adjustment.

column1: What is the period that separates short-term from long-term for listed equity shares? (verify AY)
column2: 12 months — beyond that it is long-term.

column1: Why does Section 54 exempt gains on a house reinvested in another house?
column2: The law encourages continuity of housing; if you roll the gain into a new home, you haven't cashed out, so tax is deferred/exempted.

column1: Why must the reinvestment amount under 54EC be in specified bonds within 6 months? (verify AY)
column2: The exemption channels gains into nation-building infrastructure bonds; the time limit ensures prompt reinvestment, not indefinite deferral.

column1: Why is the Capital Gains Account Scheme needed at all?
column2: If you can't reinvest before the return due date, parking funds in the CGAS preserves the exemption while you complete the purchase/construction in time.

column1: Why is "transfer" defined so broadly for capital gains?
column2: To catch economic substance — exchanges, relinquishment, extinguishment of rights — so gains aren't escaped by disguising a sale as something else.

column1: Why does Section 56(2)(x) tax gifts received without consideration above a threshold? (verify AY)
column2: To plug the gap where untaxed money moves as "gifts"; receipts above 50,000 from non-relatives are taxed as Other Sources.

column1: Why are gifts from relatives or on marriage exempt under 56(2)(x)?
column2: These reflect genuine personal relationships, not income-shifting, so the law carves them out from the anti-abuse provision.

column1: Why is clubbing of income (Sec 60-64) required?
column2: To stop tax avoidance by diverting income to a spouse/minor in a lower slab; the income is clubbed back with the real earner.

column1: Why is a minor child's income clubbed with the higher-earning parent? (verify AY)
column2: A minor can't independently earn most income, so it is attributed to the parent, with a small exemption per child to avoid harshness.

column1: Why can business losses be carried forward but not set off against salary?
column2: To prevent taxpayers from sheltering salary with business losses; the law ring-fences business losses to business income within the carry-forward window.

column1: Why can unabsorbed depreciation be carried forward indefinitely, unlike business loss?
column2: Depreciation is a mandatory statutory allowance, not a discretionary loss, so it is treated more leniently with no time cap and no return-filing condition.

column1: Why must a return be filed on time to carry forward most losses?
column2: Timely filing is the compliance price of the carry-forward benefit; late filers forfeit it (except unabsorbed depreciation and house property loss).

column1: Why does Chapter VI-A cap total deductions at gross total income?
column2: Deductions are reliefs from income, not a source of refund; they cannot create or increase a loss, so they stop at reducing GTI to nil.

column1: Why does 80C reward specified savings/investments? (verify AY)
column2: To channel household savings into long-term instruments (PF, LIC, ELSS, principal repayment) with a combined cap of 1.5 lakh.

column1: Why is 80D (health insurance) separate from 80C? (verify AY)
column2: Health cover is socially prioritised, so it gets its own limit rather than competing with the crowded 80C basket.

column1: Why does 80TTA/80TTB give interest deductions, and who gets which? (verify AY)
column2: To give small relief on bank interest — 80TTA (savings interest) for general taxpayers, 80TTB (broader, higher) for senior citizens.

column1: Why does a rebate under 87A fully eliminate tax for small incomes rather than just reduce the rate? (verify AY)
column2: It targets the lowest earners for full relief up to a threshold, keeping them out of the tax net entirely without changing the slab structure.

column1: Why is surcharge "a tax on tax" levied only above high income thresholds? (verify AY)
column2: It adds progressivity at the top by charging extra on the tax amount of high earners, without disturbing lower slabs.

column1: Why does marginal relief exist for surcharge?
column2: To ensure that crossing a surcharge threshold by a small amount doesn't increase tax by more than the extra income — preventing an unfair cliff.

column1: Why is Health & Education Cess charged on tax plus surcharge? (verify AY)
column2: It is an earmarked levy (currently 4%) funding health and education, applied on the aggregated tax to spread the cost across all taxpayers.

column1: Why does the new tax regime offer lower rates but fewer deductions?
column2: It trades away exemptions for simplicity and lower slabs, letting taxpayers who don't invest heavily pay less with no paperwork.

column1: Why is TDS deducted at source rather than collected at year-end?
column2: To secure revenue early, widen the tax base, and create an audit trail — tax is collected as income arises, reducing evasion and default.

column1: Why does TDS on salary use the average rate over the year?
column2: Salary is spread across months, so the employer estimates annual tax and deducts it evenly, avoiding a lump-sum shock at year-end.

column1: What is the consequence under 234B and 234C, and why two sections?
column2: 234B charges interest for not paying 90% advance tax; 234C for missing quarterly instalments — separating the failure to pay from the failure to pay on time.

column1: Why is advance tax paid in instalments during the year? (verify AY)
column2: Income accrues through the year, so tax is matched to it in quarterly instalments (15%/45%/75%/100%), keeping government cash flow steady.

column1: Why is interest under 234A charged for late filing of return?
column2: It compensates the government for delayed self-assessment tax remaining unpaid past the due date until the return is filed.

column1: Why does GST replace multiple indirect taxes with one?
column2: To remove the cascading of tax-on-tax across VAT, excise, and service tax, creating a single seamless value-added tax with full input credit.

column1: Why is GST called a "destination-based consumption tax"?
column2: Tax accrues to the state where goods/services are consumed, not produced, so revenue follows demand rather than manufacturing location.

column1: Why does GST split into CGST + SGST for intra-state and IGST for inter-state?
column2: Intra-state supply is shared between Centre and State (CGST+SGST); inter-state is a single IGST that the Centre later apportions to the consuming state.

column1: Why is "supply" the taxable event in GST rather than sale or manufacture?
column2: Supply is broader — it captures sale, transfer, barter, lease, and disposal — so the trigger covers all commercial dealings under one concept.

column1: Why does Schedule I tax certain supplies even without consideration?
column2: To catch value transfers like related-party supplies and permanent asset disposals with ITC, preventing tax leakage through "free" transactions.

column1: Why is the place of supply critical in GST?
column2: It determines whether a supply is intra- or inter-state, which decides CGST+SGST vs IGST and which state gets the revenue.

column1: Why is time of supply needed in GST?
column2: It fixes the point when tax liability arises (earliest of invoice, payment, or receipt), so returns and payment happen in the right period.

column1: What is the Input Tax Credit mechanism and why does it prevent cascading?
column2: ITC lets a registered person offset tax paid on inputs against tax on outputs, so tax applies only to value added at each stage.

column1: Why are the four conditions for claiming ITC (Sec 16) strict? (verify AY)
column2: Possession of tax invoice, receipt of goods/services, tax actually paid to government, and return filed — ensuring credit only where tax genuinely reached the exchequer.

column1: Why is ITC blocked on items like personal cars and club memberships (Sec 17(5))?
column2: These are prone to personal use, not business value addition, so credit is denied to stop diversion of business credit to consumption.

column1: Why must ITC be reversed if payment to supplier isn't made within 180 days?
column2: ITC presupposes the transaction is real and paid; unpaid invoices suggest the value wasn't actually incurred, so the credit is clawed back.

column1: Why does the Composition Scheme trade lower rates for no ITC? (verify AY)
column2: Small taxpayers get a simple flat rate on turnover and minimal compliance, but forgo input credit and can't collect tax from customers.

column1: Why can't a composition dealer make inter-state outward supplies?
column2: The scheme is meant for small local businesses; inter-state supply implies wider operations that belong under the regular regime.

column1: Why is the GST registration threshold different for goods vs services? (verify AY)
column2: Goods get a higher threshold (e.g. 40 lakh) than services (20 lakh) because service providers add value with lower turnover, warranting earlier registration.

column1: Why is registration mandatory regardless of turnover for inter-state suppliers?
column2: Inter-state trade involves IGST and cross-state revenue apportionment, so the government requires registration to track it from the first rupee.

column1: Why does Reverse Charge Mechanism shift tax liability to the recipient?
column2: For hard-to-track suppliers (unregistered persons, specified services), collecting from the organised recipient is more reliable than from the supplier.

column1: Why can a supply be "composite" vs "mixed", and why does it matter?
column2: Composite = naturally bundled (taxed at principal supply's rate); mixed = artificially bundled (taxed at the highest rate) — classification drives the applicable rate.

column1: Why is a tax invoice mandatory under GST?
column2: It is the primary document evidencing supply and enabling the recipient's ITC; without it, the credit chain breaks.

column1: Why does an e-way bill exist for movement of goods above a threshold? (verify AY)
column2: To track goods in transit, curb evasion, and verify that tax-paid goods match declared supplies during movement.

column1: Why is a Bill of Supply issued instead of a tax invoice by composition/exempt suppliers?
column2: They cannot charge GST, so they issue a Bill of Supply that carries no tax component, signalling no ITC is available.

column1: Why is GSTR-1 (outward) reconciled against GSTR-3B and 2B?
column2: To ensure the tax declared on sales, the summary return, and the recipient's available credit all match — enforcing the self-policing credit chain.

column1: Why is exempt supply different from zero-rated supply in GST?
column2: Exempt supply carries no tax and blocks ITC; zero-rated (exports/SEZ) is taxed at 0% but allows ITC — so exporters get refunds, exempt sellers don't.

column1: Why are exports treated as zero-rated rather than exempt?
column2: To keep Indian goods globally competitive by refunding all embedded taxes, so tax is not exported along with the goods.

column1: Why does GST allow a refund of accumulated ITC in inverted duty structures?
column2: When inputs are taxed higher than outputs, credit piles up unusable; refund releases the blocked working capital.

column1: Why is TDS under GST (Sec 51) applied to certain government contracts? (verify AY)
column2: To ensure tax on large public-sector supplies is captured at source from deductors, improving compliance visibility.

column1: Why does TCS under GST (Sec 52) apply to e-commerce operators?
column2: The operator collects tax on supplies made through its platform, bringing numerous small online sellers into the tax net via a single collector.

column1: Why does the GST law prescribe a formal valuation (Sec 15) based on transaction value?
column2: Tax must be on the real price paid between unrelated parties; transaction value anchors it, with adjustments only where price is influenced or incomplete.

column1: Why are subsidies from the government excluded from GST taxable value?
column2: Government subsidies aren't part of the consideration between supplier and buyer, so they don't represent the price of the supply.

column1: Why is interest on delayed GST payment charged on the net cash liability? (verify AY)
column2: Interest compensates only for tax actually withheld from the government; since ITC was already with the exchequer, interest applies to the net cash shortfall.

column1: Why does a debit/credit note adjust GST rather than reissuing an invoice?
column2: It corrects value or tax post-invoice (returns, discounts, errors) while preserving the original invoice trail for audit.

column1: Why must books of account be maintained even under presumptive taxation if income is declared lower? (verify AY)
column2: Declaring below the presumptive rate rebuts the presumption, so the taxpayer must prove the lower figure with books and audit.

column1: Why is the concept of "aggregate turnover" used for GST thresholds?
column2: It sums all taxable, exempt, export, and inter-state supplies PAN-India, giving a true picture of scale to test registration and composition eligibility.

column1: Why does Section 194 series prescribe different TDS rates for different payments?
column2: Each payment type (rent, contract, professional fees, interest) has a different margin and risk of non-reporting, so rates are calibrated per stream. (verify AY)

column1: Why is a Permanent Account Number (PAN) linked to higher TDS if not furnished? (verify AY)
column2: Without PAN the deductee can't be tracked, so a penal higher rate (e.g. 20%) both compensates risk and pressures PAN compliance.

column1: Why does income deemed to accrue in India (Sec 9) tax non-residents on Indian-source income?
column2: The source rule lets India tax income economically connected to India (business connection, Indian property, salary for services in India) regardless of residence.

column1: Why is a slab-based rate structure used for individuals rather than a flat rate?
column2: Progressive slabs tax higher incomes at higher rates, aligning the burden with ability to pay — a core equity principle.

column1: Why is a firm/company taxed at a flat rate rather than slabs?
column2: Entities don't have "subsistence needs" like individuals, so a single rate applies to their whole profit without a personal exemption threshold. (verify AY)

column1: Why is set-off of losses done intra-head before inter-head?
column2: You first net gains and losses within the same head (same nature), then allow the residual loss to relieve other heads — a structured cascade.

column1: Why can speculative business losses only be set off against speculative profits?
column2: Speculation is high-risk and distinct, so the law quarantines its losses to prevent them from eroding normal business or other income.

column1: Why is capital loss segregated into short-term and long-term for set-off?
column2: LTCL can offset only LTCG (both taxed gently), while STCL can offset either — matching the character and rate of the loss to the gain.

column1: Why does the Income Tax Act tax perquisites in addition to salary?
column2: Non-cash benefits (rent-free housing, cars, ESOPs) are real economic gains from employment, so they're valued and taxed to prevent salary being disguised as perks.

column1: Why is an employer's PF contribution above a limit taxable to the employee? (verify AY)
column2: Beyond the exempt ceiling it becomes a real accretion to the employee's wealth, so the excess loses its retirement-savings shelter and is taxed.

column1: Why does the law distinguish "revenue" from "capital" receipts for taxability?
column2: Revenue receipts (recurring, from operations) are income; capital receipts (one-off, from the profit-earning structure) are generally outside income tax unless specifically charged.

column1: Why is entertainment allowance deductible only for government employees? (verify AY)
column2: It is a legacy concession limited to government service; private employees get no such deduction, reflecting the provision's historical scope.

column1: Why must GST returns be filed even in a nil-activity period?
column2: The self-assessment system needs continuous declarations to keep the credit chain and compliance record intact; a nil return confirms no suppressed activity.

column1: Why does the GST Council, not Parliament alone, decide rates?
column2: GST is a shared Centre-State tax, so a joint federal body (the Council) sets rates to preserve cooperative federalism and uniformity.

column1: Why is the anti-profiteering provision built into GST?
column2: To ensure that rate cuts and ITC benefits are passed to consumers as lower prices, not pocketed by businesses as extra margin.
